Specified prerequisite -equivalent courses may require a "C" grade to serve as the equivalent prerequisite at the receiving institution; for non -equivalent prerequisite courses, a higher grade may be required.
Pass/Fail Credit The application of pass/fail grading systems to transfer students shall be consistent with the application of those systems to students who entered the institution as freshmen.
Transfer students should consult the catalog of the in stitution to which they are transferring regarding these policies.
Non-Traditional Learning and Evaluation for Credit The determination of the credit value of non -traditional learning is typically achieved through an examination or other standardized or institutionally- accepted form of assessing prior learning.
An institution which examines or otherwise assesses extra- institutional learning shall clearly state its criteria for measuring and awarding credit and publish information about its credit by examin ation/assessment policies in its official catalog.

For credit by examination, information must be available that includes names of tests for which credit by examination is given (Advanced Placement, general and subject matter CLEP, ACT, institutional, etc. ), and score levels which indicate that course work requirements comparable to classroom situations have been met.
For the College -Level Examination Program (CLEP), the receiving institution will accept the American Council on Education (ACE) recommended c redit- granting score for the year in which the examination was taken.
Credit awarded through examination or other forms of assessment shall be identified as such on the transcript.
These transcripted credits will be honored by the receiving institution.
Graduate and Advanced Professional Credit Decisions regarding the transfer of credit toward advanced degrees (master's, CAGS, doctorate) or advanced professional degrees rests with the faculty of the degree -granting division. 164

Resolution of Equivalency Disput es From time to time there may be interinstitutional disagreements among the faculty of subject matter disciplines.
These disagreements will normally be resolved at the chairperson level.
Conflicts not resolved by the chairperson will be referred to the Articulation/Transfer Committee.
The committee will resolve the dispute or forward a recommendation to the Postsecondary Education Executive Council (PEEC).
PEEC may accept the recommendation or seek an alternate resolution.
I V.
Transfer Guide Interinstitutional agreements on course and program equivalencies shall appear in appropriate institutional publications and be compiled regularly in a single document entitled: Transfer Guide for Students (hereafter, the guide).
The guide is an integral part of the ar ticulation/transfer policy and procedures and shall be made available for use by students, faculty and staff.
Course Equivalencies The institutions shall identify specific courses that are equivalent.
This identification shall be on a discipline -by-discipline basis and shall appear in the guide.

Information about course additions, changes or deletions by an institution shall be communicated by the appropriate chairperson to the corresponding chairpersons at other institutions for equivalency evaluation before or during the annual meeting of departmental chairs.
Program Equivalencies The institutions shall specify transfer agreements on a program -to-program basis; these agreements shall appear in the guide.
Program transfer plans will consist of the sequence of courses to be completed to fulfill associate degree requirements at the community college and the equivalent sequences at the college and the university, where appropriate.
Chairpersons shall agree on program- to-program equivalencies before or during the annual meeting of department chairs.
General Education Requirements General education programs are determined by individual institutions, each of which has the continuing responsibility for determining the character of its own program, for its own degree purposes.
General education program requirements shall be clearly stated in the institutional catalog and in the guide.

Students who intend to transfer to another institution shoul d review that institution's general education requirements and discuss their plans with admissions counselors or advisors in their intended majors.
V.
Student Rights and Responsibilities Students who intend to transfer must inform themselves of the transfer admission requirements, and the program and degree requirements of the in stitution to which they expect to transfer.
Students who through no fault of their own encounter legitimate difficulties in transferring from one institution to another must seek resolution of these difficulties through institutional procedures, with the a ssistance of academic advisors.
Students who have exhausted all administrative remedies available at the institution to which transfer credit is being sought and who have been unable to satisfactorily resolve the problem may appeal in writing to the articu lation/transfer officer at the institution that awarded the credit.

The articulation/transfer officer shall receive and consider all relevant materials and shall review the cases with appropriate representatives of the receiving institution so that a determination may be made as to the transferability of the courses or earned credits being contested. 165

Cases which cannot be satisfactorily resolved may be reviewed by the Articulation/ Transfer Committee.
When a student transfers under the course -to-course option, the articulation/ transfer agreement in place when that student initiates the second half of the associate's degree program (31 credit hours or more) will be the agreement that governs course equivalencies for that student.
When a student transfers und er a program-to-program agreement, the student is governed by the requirements in effect at the beginning of the academic year in which the student was officially accepted into the program.
These requirements will remain in effect for that student for five years regardless of changes to individual course equivalencies.
VI.
Interinstitutional Articulation/Transfer Committee Composition of the Committee To assure compliance with and the continuing viability of the Articulation/Transfer Policy, a permanent int erinstitutional committee on articulation/transfer was established.

This Articulation/Transfer Committee is comprised of eleven members: three from each of the three public institutions of higher education plus a chairperson and a staff person from the Rhode Island Office of Higher Education (RIOHE).
The institutional representatives are appointed by the president and are to include the institutional articulation/transfer officer.
The chairperson is appointed by the Commissioner of Higher Education.
Committ ee appointments shall be reviewed every three years.
Committee Responsibilities The Committee is responsible to the Postsecondary Education Executive Council (PEEC) for the following tasks: * Soliciting suggestions from administrators, faculty and students matters of articulation/transfer; * Providing continuous evaluation and review of institutional programs, policies and procedures, and interinstitutional relationships affecting transfer of students; * Recommending such revisions as are needed in institut ional programs, policies, and procedures to promote the success and general well-being of the transfer student.

The Committee shall fulfill these responsibilities in the following ways: * Recommending policy or procedural changes that would improve articul ation/transfer in higher education institutions; * Recommending resolution of course equivalency disputes between cooperating institutions; * Conducting reviews as needed of the Articulation/Transfer Policy; * Planning and executing the annual meeting of d epartment chairpersons and assisting in the production of the guide.
Committee Meetings The Articulation/Transfer Committee shall be convened, as necessary, by its chairperson.
PART II: Undergraduate Transfer Policy (Amended 1999-00) 166

The University of Rhode Island prepares a formal transfer credit evaluation only after an applicant has been accepted as a degree student.
Evaluations are prepared in a course -by-course manner with the course number and course title of the former school displayed on the left si de of the page and the University course equivalent on the right.
Most of the course evaluations are made from catalog course descriptions.
An equivalent University of Rhode Island course number is assigned wherever possible provided the other college work requires the same prerequisites as those required by University departments and provided the work is comparable in content, scope, and level to University courses.
If no equivalent URI course can be designated, departmental elective credits or free elective credits may be awarded.
A departmental elective may be used to fulfill major or minor credit requirements in the specific department, but may not be used for General Education.
A free elective fulfills credit hours needed for graduation but does not mee t department or General Education requirements.
The University usually awards the credit value of the sending institution.

Excess credits are used as free electives.
Courses taken in disciplines that are not represented at the University of Rhode Island ar e awarded free elective credit unless the courses are equivalent or nearly equivalent to courses offered by URI.
Transfer credit may be given in those courses in which the student received a grade of "C" (2.00) or better, but no credit shall be given for courses in which a "C -" or lower was earned.
However, Board of Governors Policy for Articulation/Transfer (Appendix F, Part I) mandates that college level credit earned with minimally acceptable grades at another public postsecondary education institution i n Rhode Island shall be transferable as earned credit.
Credit transferred from a community or junior college is limited only by the provision that the student must earn at least half the credits required for the University of Rhode Island degree at a bacca laureate granting institution.
No course credit earned at the University or at other institutions shall be counted for graduation after eight years, except by consent of the dean of the degree granting college involved.
Advanced Placement.

The University awards credits and/or course exemptions to freshmen and transfer students who present scores of 3 or higher on the College Board Advanced Placement Tests.
Art, Music, Theatre courses offered by an accredited institution are referred to respective department s for evaluation for students majoring in those areas.
Athletics.
The University does not grant credit for participation in intercollegiate athletics.
Business Administration Courses.
The University grants direct transfer credit for equivalent business adm inistration courses taken at institutions that are accredited by the American Assembly of Collegiate Schools of Business.
Upper level business courses taken at an institution not accredited by this Association must be validated by examination.
Those courses not validated will be awarded free elective credit.
College Level Examination Program (CLEP).
The University grants transfer credit for CLEP examinations taken prior to enrollment at the University of Rhode Island provided the scores meet University stan dards and the CLEP credit does not duplicate other transfer credit.
Regulations regarding CLEP may be found in the University Manual.

CLEP credit and score minimums are delineated in the University Catalog.
Correspondence Courses offered through an accredi ted institution shall be evaluated for transfer provided course titles, grades and credit values appear on an official college or university transcript.
Foreign Credits.
Each foreign transcript shall be evaluated independently. 167

International Baccalaureate Diploma Program.
Academic credit may be awarded for most higher level examinations passed with a score of 5, 6, or 7.
Course credit is awarded at the discretion of individual departments.
The University grants no credit for standard level examinations.
Non-collegiate Educational Experiences.
Academic credit may be awarded for knowledge and skills gained in non - collegiate settings.
Only assessment procedures approved by academic departments, colleges and the Faculty Senate may be used.
Pass/Fail Courses.
The University accepts credits offered by an accredited institution that were taken on a pass/fail basis.
However, such credit cannot be used for concentration or General Education requirements.
Pre-collegiate, Remedial, Personal Development or Self -improvement Courses.
The University grants no credit for these courses.
Professional Courses. (e.g.
Computer Science, Dental Hygiene, Engineering, Medical Technology, Nursing, Pharmacy) as well as courses of an advanced nature, independent studies, practicums and seminars offered by an accredited institution shall be referred to appropriate faculty for evaluation and course equivalency.

Proficiency and Waiver Examinations.
A student who successfully passes a departmental proficiency examination shall earn credits as well as exemption from the course.
A student who successfully passes a department waiver examination shall be exempted from the course, but shall earn no credit.
Religion Courses.
Only those courses offered by accredited institutions which are planned and taught from a strictly historical, literary or comparative viewpoint as determined by the appropriate faculty shall be awarded transfer credit.
Technical, Vocational Courses.
The University grants no credit for technical or vocational courses.
College parallel courses taken at technical institutions may be granted credit.
Veterans.
The University evaluates the Formal Service Schools of veterans in accord with the recommendations of the American Council on Evaluation handbook, A Guide to the Evaluation of E xperiences in the Armed Forces and credit allowances may be granted when appropriate to the curriculum in which registration is sought. 168

CONSTITUTION, BY-LAWS, AND UNIVERSITY MANUAL COMMITTEE Report #2022-2023-7 - INFORMATIONALFACULTY SENATE, November 17, 2022 Context and rationale: At the Faculty Senate meeting on September 29, 2022, Senate leadershipshared with the community a long list of administrative policies that had been recently approved bythe Administrative Policy Committee (APC).
Senators expressed concerns about the speed at whichpolicies were being developed/revised and approved, and about the opacity with which the APCseemed to be functioning (ambiguity in University Manual language about committee membership,lack of availability of a list of current members on any URI website, lack of details available to theuniversity community about APC vetting processes, etc.).
In response to the listing of the policies onthe agenda and the brief discussion that took place, Faculty Senate President Rice asked Senators andSenate standing committees to examine the policies closely and to invite colleagues across campus todo the same.

The purpose of these efforts is to engage the faculty in administrative policydevelopment and amendment processes, to correct potential errors or flaws in new or revisedadministrative policies (conflicts with the existing duly approved administrative or academic policiesin the University Manual, areas in which all impacts appear to not have been fully considered, orother flaws), and to improve the quality of administrative policies that are ultimately adopted by thecommunity.
In response to President Rice’s request, CBUM is devoting time during each meeting to review anddiscuss policies listed on the September Faculty Senate meeting agenda.
The main aim of our scrutinyis to identify potential errors or conflicts as they relate to the duly approved statutes and policies inthe University’s primary governance document, and administrative and academic policyclearinghouse: the University Manual.
The committee has discussed three approved policies and onedraft policy; this report outlines concerns raised during those preliminary discussions about fourpolicies.
CBUM will continue the process of reviewing policies and reporting to the Senate anyconcerns raised during our discussions.

Given the daunting volume of policies requiring review,CBUM reiterates President Rice’s September call and requests that all other Senate standingcommittees, individual Senators, and the faculty that the Senate represents also contribute activelyand conscientiously to this effort. 1.
Policy 01.110.1.
Policy on adverse weather and other emergencies ○ Administrative vs. academic policy: As currently written, the policy is so expansive thatit extends beyond the appropriate administrative realm and includes academicmatters: such issues do not fall within the purview of the APC.
The decision to cancelclasses or to shift to a different instructional modality is not an administrative decision,but an academic one.

○ Chain of responsible people for academic decision-making: Although it may seemlogical for the chain of responsible people for decision-making to mimic the currentBoard of Trustees language about University officers, this chain does not seemappropriate or advisable in the case of academic decisions.
The University Manualcontains provisions for the Vice Provost for Academic and Faculty Initiatives torepresent the Office of the Provost in the absence of the Provost (2.22.11).
In the eventthat the Provost is unable to make a decision about class cancellation or a change ininstructional modality, the Vice Provost seems to be the most appropriateadministrator to make such decisions.
Recommended action: Revise the policy to eliminate all components relating to academics,faculty, and instructional modalities.
The Faculty Senate, not the APC, is the appropriate bodyto develop and approve academic policies. 2.

Policy 01.102.1 - External Speakers on Campus ○ On page 4, the conduct section states “If as a result of the presence or behavior of theSponsored Guest on University Property a protest, rally, or riot occurs or is threatened … the University has the right in its sole discretion at any time to revoke theSponsored Guest’s status and cancel the event.” ○ The inclusion of “presence” in addition to “behavior” suggests that the Universitycould cancel an event with a speaker who is controversial simply because people mightprotest the event, not because the speaker's actions incited a disturbance.
This seemsto conflict not only with the UM language on controversial persons (6.14.10-6.14.17),but also with precedent regarding free speech rights and the idea that the governmentmay not use a "heckler's veto" to justify suppressing speech.
Recommended action: Revise the policy to address the conflicts. 3.
Policy 02.103.2 - Graffiti - Graffiti is defined as "Unauthorized and unlawful writings or drawingsmade on a wall or other surface." This definition is so broad that it includes even something asbenign as using chalk to draw on walkways.

Recommended action: Revise the definition of graffiti in the policy. 4.
Draft policy on Research Misconduct ○ Administrative vs. academic policy: The draft policy focuses on academic research andethical conduct of academic research, and thus does not fall under the purview of theAPC. ○ Anonymous ethics hotline: The draft policy contains a section on an Ethics Hotline.Although the intent of this is understandable, there is concern that it could be used

unethically and inappropriately to target certain people or create difficulties for them.Because anonymous reports are allowed, there is potential for misuse. ○ Lack of vetting of the draft by research faculty: The Stakeholder Group that reviewedthis draft policy included only one faculty member. ○ Inclusion of the Faculty Senate among the entities that, as of October 11, 2022, had“reviewed” the draft policy: The draft policy was included on the Faculty SenateSeptember meeting agenda for the purpose of making the community aware of thevolume of policies that the APC was developing and approving and the speed at whichthe APC was doing this work. The Faculty Senate did not review, discuss, or approve thedraft policy: the Faculty Senate leadership requested that Senators, committees, andindividual members of the faculty review this draft policy (and all other policies listedon the agenda) and bring forward concerns in the future. Recommended action: Refer this draft policy in its entirety to the Faculty Senate: the FacultySenate, not the APC, is the appropriate body to work with the President, the Vice President ofResearch and Economic Development, and General Counsel to revise and legislate researchpolicies.

Illinois Computing Accelerator for Non-Specialists (iCAN)

Goal: Expand the iCAN program to 20-25 students in 2021 with at least 50% of enrolled students identifying as underrepresented in computing because of their race, gender, and/or disability status.
Activities: To broaden access to computing for people with a bachelor’s degree in any field other than CS, we created iCAN, which launched in the fall of 2020. iCAN’s mission is to broaden participation in computing through an accelerated program for non-CS college graduates. The inaugural class has 7 students, 57% of whom are from groups underrepresented in computing because of their gender and/or race. We seek to expand to 20-25 students, and apply to enable students to be eligible for federal student loans to make the program more accessible (Williams, Amato, Viswanathan).
Collect and Analyze Data: Retention
Goal: In 2020-2021, identify rates of attrition among CS majors to guide our 2021-2022 BPC Plan.
Activities: To better understand attrition within our BS programs, we will identify our attrition rates disaggregated by race, ethnicity, gender, and first-generation college status (Chacko). These data will inform the BPC plan for 2021-2022, but will not necessarily be shared.

Collect and Analyze Data: Data Buddies Survey
Goal: In 2020-2021, expand student participation in the Data Buddies Survey to at least 500 undergraduate students and 300 graduate students. (Previously 172 and 176, respectively).
Activities: To better understand our students’ experiences, we seek to increase our student’s participation in the annual Data Buddies survey, which disaggregates data by gender and race. We plan to (1) offer a raffle (Lewis), (2) promote the survey with our student groups (Coleman), (3) share email and presentation templates with faculty (Amato), and (4) promote the survey in weekly department emails that students receive (Harris). In the Spring of 2021, we will review our Data Buddies Survey report in a departmental faculty meeting.
Student Community Organization
Goal: Provide student organizations transparency into and a voice in departmental BPC efforts.

Activities: To have students’ priorities drive our BPC efforts, we have student representation on our BPC committee and we will solicit suggestions of BPC initiatives at the monthly CS Student Leadership Council (CSSLC) meetings (Coleman/Amato/Harris). We have a thriving set of student organizations that are represented at the CSSLC meetings (e.g., Blacks and African Americans in Computing, Latinxs in Computer Science, Women in Computer Science, WiCyS, AI4ALL, and Hack4Impact). At the CSSLC meetings, students will also be encouraged to attend the Department Head’s weekly open office hours to share additional suggestions. To provide transparency to students, we will also present updates from the BPC committee with particular attention to how student suggestions have shaped the committee’s work.
Faculty and Staff BPC Education
Goal: Encourage faculty and staff participation in opportunities to learn about BPC and racism.

Activities: To increase faculty and staff knowledge of BPC and racism more generally, we will encourage participation in relevant workshops and seminars. Faculty will be asked to report their participation in their annual faculty reports. In the fall of 2020, we started the monthly speaker series “Illinois Computer Science Conversations on Equity & Justice in Computing.” This supplements workshops and seminars hosted by the Office of the Vice Chancellor for Diversity, Equity, & Inclusion and the Grainger College of Engineering Institute for Inclusion, Diversity, Equity, and Access. We will promote at least one event in each “Inside CS Weekly Digest” (Harris).

PROGRAM REPORT CURRICULUM & STANDARDS COMMITTEE Report 2025-2026-08B At the April 23, 2026 meeting of the Curriculum & Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval.
FOR CONFIRMATION BY THE FACULTY SENATE COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES BA – Computer Science, effective Fall 2026 Appendix A This curriculum revision represents a strategic modernization that strengthens the B.A. in Computer Science through internal reallocation of Department resources while preserving its distinctive character as a flexible, interdisciplinary degree option.
The proposed changes maintain 120 total credits while prescribing a 36-credit core.
The B.A. requires nine core CS courses compared to eleven core and three specialization courses in the B.S. program, providing a lighter computing load while ensuring foundational competency in software development, algorithms, systems, and machine learning.
BA – Film Media, effective Summer 2026 Appendix B Film media is deleting courses that have been removed from the URI catalog and adding new FLM courses to the appropriate elective pools.

BA – Journalism, effective Fall 2026 Appendix C During a curriculum retreat, members of the journalism faculty evaluated both the program learning outcomes and the curriculum for the B.A in Journalism degree program.
Based on our retreat and our focus on experiential learning in the program, we voted to adopt new requirements for our major.
These changes include eliminating the conceptual/skills designation in our current curriculum, adding additional core requirements, and altering JOR elective options so that students may pursue recommended, but not required, pathways in print, photojournalism, and multimedia/video journalism.
Several advanced courses will work directly with our new Community News Lab, which provides real-world experience to our students by having them produce news content for local media organizations.

BA – Public Relations, effective Fall 2026 Appendix D The Public Relations degree program was developed within the Communication Studies department.
In the Fall of 2024, the program moved into a new department.
The Department of Journalism and Public Relations now manages both the Journalism BA and Public Relations BA degrees.
While the PR program stands on its own, it shares many courses with Communication Studies, particularly in the three focus areas.
As the two programs have become more distinct, scheduling and course management issues have arisen.
Public Relations majors have trouble enrolling in Communication Studies courses to fulfill their focus areas.
We are proposing to amend the focus areas so s tudents have more flexibility in their elective courses.
Both the JOR/PR faculty and the Communication Studies faculty support the proposed changes (please see attached).
Please note the focus area course list remains the same with one exception, we added an additional course COM 321G.
BA – Theatre, effective Fall 2026 Appendix E The Theatre BA is currently suspended and only open to those students who are pursuing a degree in Elementary Education.

We propose reinstating the BA for all eligible students in order to serve the shifting demographic of our student body as well as refine our BFA program to introduce more rigorous standards appropriate to a pre-professional training program.
The Rhode Island Promise Act has increased the number of transfer students considerably, making it highly difficult for those students to complete a BFA in 4 years.
Additionally, the number of double majors/minors has increased making it equally difficult for those students to complete the very narrow BFA curriculum without impact to their other majors (particularly those, such as Nursing, who also have to meet clinical requirements that tend to conflict with our required courses).
A BA offers more flexibility for order of courses, thus making it more feasible for our transfer students and those completing more than one major.
URI Theatre completed an External Review in Spring of 2024.
Among their recommendations was to standardize evaluation tools across our curriculum and instate more rigorous standards for degree completion, including capstone performances and projects.

Many BFA programs also involve standards that, if not met, result in dismissal from the program.
It has never been the policy of URI theatre to dismiss students from our program except in very rare cases of academic failure.
Introducing this type of standardization is possible if we have the option to invite students to our BA program in the event that the BFA curriculum is not a good fit.
Bifurcating our program in this way allows URI Theatre to serve the widest number of students while also introducing more clear standards for our BFA students.
The reinstatement of the BA does not require any new courses or staffing.
Students in the BA program will be taking courses already offered in our existing curriculum but have more choice in terms of when and what they take.

Because our program has undergone some changes to course codes since the suspension of the BA, we include here the courses we propose for completion of the BA in Theatre: Core Courses (total of 33 credits): THE111 (Introduction to Acting), THE161 (Introduction to Stagecraft), THE181 (Script Analysis), THE221 (Introduction to Stage Management), THE250 (Costume Laboratory), THE251 (Introduction to Design), THE307 or THE338G ( Creative Dramatics or Ethics in Theatre), THE321 (Orientation to Directing), THE381 (Theatre History to 1642), THE382 (Theatre History:

Neoclassical through 19th century), and either THE351, 352, 383, 384 OR 481 (these are advanced design or special topics courses) for a total of 33 required credits.
Optional electives within the major include THE112, THE200, THE300, THE400.
For many students, this would include participating in our production season for which they receive course credit (THE200/300/400).
Students must complete a minimum of 30 credits at the 300-level or above (these may include 300-level courses offered inside the major or courses offered outside the program).

This course would benefit our clinical neuroscience students from knowledge regarding psychotropics medications that are used to treat clinical disorders (depression, anxiety, OCD, etc.) Many of the clinical neuroscience students pursue healthcare, graduate PhD programs in psychology, and medical school.

A wide range of courses is available to the film/media student—courses that examine the historical, theoretical, and global approaches to the analysis and creation of moving images.

The film/media program prepares students for careers in such areas as independent filmmaking; animation and media design; film and television industries; advertising, marketing, and public relations; and media criticism.
Graduates of this program are also prepared to continue with graduate studies, either in film and media production for an M.F.A., or in a master’s or doctoral program in film and media studies.
Students majoring in film/media must complete a minimum of 31 credits (maximum 46) in approved courses toward the major.
FLM 101 or FLM 101H is a required prerequisite.
All students must complete the core courses: FLM 110, FLM 203 (or ENG 302), FLM 204 (or FLM 205 or 206), including the senior-level seminar FLM 495 (or FLM 496); a minimum of 6 credits from the production and technique category and 6 credits from the critical studies category; a minimum of 3 elective credits in courses that count toward the film major from the Production and Technique and Critical Studies categories (see below).
This wide range of choices in film/media courses permits students to design a major that will meet both personal and professional goals.

Students must have a plan of study approved by an academic advisor in the film media program before beginning their coursework in the major.
